source.title: Learning Rates for Stochastic Gradient Descent With Nonconvex Objectives

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test-set gradient error and how it changes with SGD step-size schedules, using a different task and measure from the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports simulation results on three datasets. It does not test random-label memorization, network width or architecture, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, sharpness, or example removal.
record.test_reason: The study cites original generalization papers as motivation, but its own theory and simulations test none of V1–V8. It studies SGD convergence and test-set gradient norms for logistic-link generalized linear models, comparing learning-rate schedules rather than any intervention or measure specified by the versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the authors derive high-probability learning bounds by jointly controlling optimization and statistical errors, explain how iteration count balances them, and obtain dimension-independent bounds for structured losses. These results concern population gradients generally and excess risk under additional gradient-dominance assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The simulations use a logistic-link generalized linear model on LIBSVM datasets and compare polynomial step-size schedules; the listed versions concern other interventions, models, or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Test errors differed across step-size exponents: θ = 1/2 outperformed θ = 0 and θ = 1 in the reported experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6 reports that the inverse-square-root learning-rate schedule outperforms constant and inverse-time schedules in test-set gradient norm on Segment, Fourclass, and German, with initial learning rates selected by validation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For these logistic-link generalized linear models and tested schedules, inverse-square-root SGD gives better held-out gradient convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6 and Figure 1 report decreasing training gradient norms, increasing train–test gradient discrepancies, and stable test gradient norms through 200 passes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training and statistical gradient errors can move in opposite directions while held-out gradient norms remain stable during prolonged SGD training.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The simulation evidence is limited to three datasets and logistic-link binary classification. Fig. 2 provides the schedule comparison, but the text gives no numerical test-error values or uncertainty for that comparison.

untested.parts: All parts: fitting random labels and comparing natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy under matched architectures and recipes.
All parts: network width, interpolation, and test error beyond the width needed to fit.
All parts: convolutional versus fully connected networks, local connectivity, and initialization effects.
All parts: adaptive versus SGD optimizers and the effects of tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
All parts: batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
All parts: dropout, training-set size, underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
All parts: magnitude-aware weight perturbations, their association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
All parts: identifying memorized examples and comparing their removal with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Small held-out gradient norm indicates approximate stationarity, not necessarily low classification error or high accuracy. Figure 2's numerical curves are not available in the supplied text; its qualitative schedule comparison is stated explicitly. The simulations average 100 repetitions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap.
Removal of memorized examples and its effect on test accuracy.
